headline: High: Continue’s filesystem/MCP access can feed Taipy workflows, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action risks in default IDE setups.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Continue can read workspace files and use MCP, and its shared state is via filesystem; Taipy is a data-engineering automation app that may consume files or workflow inputs. That creates a plausible injection bridge if Taipy ingests Continue-authored content as instructions. The pairwise pathway is inferred, not directly documented, so I choose medium over low.
conditions: IF Taipy ingests files or text produced by Continue without sanitization
IF a shared workspace or MCP bridge passes attacker-controlled content from Continue into Taipy
mitigations: Disable shared filesystem handoff between the tools
Require content-type or schema validation on Taipy inputs
Strip instruction-like text before Taipy parses Continue outputs
Use separate workspaces per agent
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for all inter-agent messages

B_data_leakage.rationale: Continue reads workspace files and editor buffers and has broad network egress; Taipy is docs-only with no declared egress, but its data-engineering role implies it may process the same files. If sensitive source code or buffers flow from Continue into Taipy, leakage can occur through Taipy outputs or logs. The exact transfer path is undocumented, so uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF both agents access the same workspace files
IF Taipy logs or exports data derived from Continue-read buffers
mitigations: Keep sensitive files out of the shared workspace
Turn off or minimize Continue network egress where possible
Review Taipy logging and export settings before use
Use separate OS users or containers
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Continue explicitly writes the filesystem and shares state via filesystem across instances; Taipy is a data-engineering/automation tool that commonly mutates datasets or workflow artifacts. Even without explicit Taipy write permissions in the profile, the pair can contend over shared mutable files, and uncertainty about Taipy’s write surface escalates the risk. I choose high because the shared-write pathway may corrupt work products.
conditions: IF Taipy writes to any file or dataset also edited by Continue
IF both agents operate in the same directory without locking
mitigations: Assign separate directories for each agent
Add file locks around shared artifacts
Pause one agent while the other writes
Use versioned copies instead of in-place edits
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: Continue produces chat and autocomplete outputs, and Taipy is an automation-oriented data-engineering tool that could treat upstream outputs as workflow inputs. If Taipy consumes Continue’s text without verification, a mistaken or malicious suggestion can cascade into downstream actions. Because Taipy’s action-taking behavior is not directly documented here, medium is the safest supported severity.
conditions: IF Taipy uses Continue output as authoritative workflow input
IF no validation step checks Continue-generated facts before execution
mitigations: Insert a human review step before Taipy actions
Validate Continue outputs against schemas or tests
Limit Taipy to read-only preview mode initially
Log provenance for every upstream field
requires-engineering: add automated verification gates

E_compliance.rationale: Continue is an IDE assistant that handles source code and editor buffers, while Taipy is open-source with no declared sensitive-data classes or residency constraints. The profiles do not show a concrete residency or certification mismatch, so only a low compliance concern remains from possible policy gaps around code and logs. I do not cite Taipy-specific compliance fields because none are declared.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into Continue-managed buffers
IF Taipy stores or logs that regulated data under a different retention policy
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in shared workspaces
Check retention settings for both tools
Disable verbose logging where possible
Document data-handling responsibilities
requires-engineering: align retention and deletion workflows
